title: Numerals

objectives.can: Read cardinal and ordinal numbers and decline unus, duo, tres and mille.

explanation.summary: Latin has two sets of numbers: cardinals (one, two, three) and ordinals (first, second, third). Only a few of them change their endings, but those few, *unus*, *duo* and *tres*, are among the commonest words in the Bible, and the ordinals and the hundreds decline like adjectives you already know. The great totals of Numbers and Ezra show them all at work.

sections.heading: Cardinals: most do not change
body: The cardinals from four to a hundred (*quatuor*, *quinque*, *septem*, *decem*, *duodecim*, *viginti*, *triginta*, *quadraginta*, *quinquaginta*, *centum*) do not decline: one form serves for every case, number and gender. The analyser therefore gives them no case at all, and the learner has to read the case from the noun they accompany.

Only the first three cardinals decline, and the hundreds from two hundred upwards (*ducenti*, *trecenti*, *quadringenti*, *quingenti*, *sescenti*, *septingenti*, *octingenti*) decline as the plural of *bonus*: masculine -i, feminine -ae, neuter -a, and so on (*trecentos*, *trecenta*). The edition spells 'four' *quatuor*; the classical spelling is *quattuor*, and you will meet both in the library.

sections.heading: unus, duo and tres
body: *unus* ('one') declines like a first and second declension adjective, with one oddity that it shares with several pronouns: its genitive singular ends in -ius (*unius*) and its dative singular in -i, in all genders. In the plural *unus* means 'alone' or 'some'.

*duo* ('two') is a plural word only. Its masculine accusative is *duos* (or *duo*), its feminine *duas* (or *duae* in the nominative), and the genitive plural *duorum* or *duarum*. The dative and ablative are *duobus* in the masculine and neuter and *duabus* in the feminine. *tres* ('three') is declined like the plural of a third-declension adjective: *tres* for the masculine and feminine, *tria* for the neuter, *trium* in the genitive, and *tribus* in the dative and ablative. It has no separate feminine.

sections.heading: Ordinals and the thousands
body: The ordinals decline exactly like *bonus*, with endings -us, -a, -um: *quartus*, *quarta*, *quartum*. They are adjectives, and they agree with their noun in case, number and gender: *dies quartus*, 'the fourth day'. The ordinals are used for days, years and the order of things.

'Thousand' is different. In the singular *mille* does not decline and is used as an adjective: 'a thousand'. In the plural it is a neuter noun, *millia*, 'thousands', and the thing counted stands in the genitive: *quadraginta sex millia*, 'forty-six thousands' (of men understood). The library files *millia* under the headword *mille* and tags it as a noun, with the genitive *millium* and the dative and ablative *millibus*.

sections.heading: Putting numbers together
body: A compound number is built by placing the parts side by side, usually largest first in Biblical Latin: 'forty-six thousand five hundred' is written *quadraginta sex millia quingenti*. Only the parts that decline change their ending. In Numbers 1 the totals of each tribe follow this pattern, and the lists show how the parts agree: *quingenti* stands in the nominative because the total is the subject of an understood verb.
The adverbs *semel* ('once') and *bis* ('twice') answer the question 'how many times'. Do not confuse them with the cardinals.

misunderstandings: *duo* is not singular, though it means 'two'. It is a plural word, and the nouns that go with it are plural: *duos fratres*.
*tres* is both nominative and accusative in the masculine and feminine, so *tres* alone does not show its case. The noun it goes with, or the sentence, does.

*millia* is not an adjective. When the number is thousands in the plural, the noun counted goes into the genitive: *millia hominum*, 'thousands of men'. The cardinals from four to a hundred do not decline at all.
A number that does not decline is not a word without a case in the sentence. In *quadraginta homines* the number has no ending to show it, but it still has the case of the noun it counts.

deeper.heading: Roman numerals in the texts
body: Some of the library's texts, especially the Fathers, also give numbers as Roman numerals (V, X, XII). These are the numbers of the same words written in a shorthand; the analyser tags them as numerals with no case.

quoted.title: 2 Corinthians
quoted.english: Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you: In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word stand.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *duorum* is the genitive plural of *duo* and *trium* the genitive plural of *tres*; both go with *testium*, 'of two or three witnesses'. The genitive plural of *duo* has the endings of the second declension, -orum; *trium* ends in -ium, like a third-declension i-stem.

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: For where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *tres* here is nominative plural, agreeing with the understood subject of *sunt*, 'two or three are gathered'. The ending alone cannot tell nominative from accusative, since both are *tres*; the verb shows that this is the subject. (The analyser does not decide the preceding *duo*, so only *tres* is marked.)
